title: To live is Christ (Philippians 1:12–26)
hook: his chains have spread the news; to live is Christ, to die is gain

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prisoner opened his letter with thanks. Your line: every remembrance. This week: peace in a locked room, Thomas, breakfast, feed my sheep, the end of John, a thank-you from prison, and now chains turned into a pulpit.

Chains, and a guard who never leaves. In this letter Paul calls them his bonds, and he is plainly under guard. Every visitor is seen. Every letter he dictates, someone overhears. Every prayer, too. Plenty of people would call that the end of their work. Paul looks at the same situation and sees an audience. The friends at Philippi are worried about him, so he writes to tell them how it's actually going.

In the King James Bible: "the things which happened unto me have fallen out rather unto the furtherance of the gospel." The prison has helped, not hurt. "So that my bonds in Christ are manifest in all the palace." Palace here is the praetorium, the Roman guard or the governor's headquarters. The whole guard knows why he's chained, and other believers, seeing him unafraid, have grown bolder. Then something surprising. Some are preaching Christ out of rivalry, hoping to make his chains hurt more. His response? "What then? notwithstanding, every way, whether in pretence, or in truth, Christ is preached; and I therein do rejoice." He doesn't need to be the hero of the story. Then the line in today's title: "For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain." He's thinking out loud about his own trial. If he lives, he keeps working, which for him is Christ. If he dies, he's with Christ, which he calls far better. "I am in a strait betwixt two": hemmed in on both sides, pulled two ways. Then he chooses, as far as it's his choice: to stay is more needful for you. He'll live for them. The passage is honest. It doesn't pretend death is nothing. It says a life wrapped around something larger is a life even prison can't shrink.
screen: then, large: `FOR TO ME TO LIVE IS CHRIST, AND TO DIE IS GAIN.`

segments.voice: Name one thing hemming you in right now, a job you can't leave yet, an illness, caring for a parent, money, a season of waiting, and look at it honestly without pretending it's good. Then ask who is around you inside it that you wouldn't meet otherwise, and what you can do here that you couldn't anywhere else. If you pray, offer the constraint to God.
Praetorium. The Roman governor's headquarters where Paul's guard is stationed, so the whole guard knows why he's chained.
Your line: a strait betwixt two. Pulled two ways, he chose the people who needed him. Another week on the path.

howItsDone: Some Christians facing illness, prison or danger turn to Philippians 1:21, and it is sometimes read at Christian funerals.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about not fearing death.
what it means: a prisoner weighing life and death honestly, and choosing to live for his friends.
what a scholar hears: praetorium (1:13), which some take as the guard in Rome and others as a governor's headquarters elsewhere, part of the debate about where Paul was held.

chat.says: How could Paul be glad in prison when rivals were preaching just to hurt him?
options: He said Christ is preached either way, and in that he rejoiced.
He wasn't glad; he wrote to ask the church to silence those preachers.
He was glad because the rivals were soon thrown in prison too.
chat.meaning: Philippians 1:18: whether in pretence or in truth, Christ is preached, and I therein do rejoice. He didn't need to be the hero.

notes: Roman custodia militaris with a prisoner chained to a soldier in shifts (cf. Acts 28:16, 20): guards taking turns is a commentary commonplace; no shift length is given. Confirm.
praetorium: guard or headquarters; location debated. Confirm.
'Pretence' is KJV spelling inside a quotation.
